entries.body: A rolly, noisy night with very little wind, we did manage to keep moving under Aries. There were several wind shifts — at one point we were heading back to Darwin! A bit confusing for Brian on his watch. No one else around. Today the wind has been picking up steadily. The swell from the south is annoying. Now it's 20 knots, broad reaching, 5–6 knots.

Wind finally picked up last night after dark and we reefed and reefed and reefed down to little jib and double-reefed main, still doing 7 knots. Not so bad except when the occasional big wave comes through. Boom vang broke last night at the bail attached to the boom. A piece of spectra took care of it. Tranquility left yesterday, 120 miles behind us, Anke 2 with Dietmar and Moonlight with Leo are ahead of us. Lots of waves with whitecaps, clear blue sky, not much else.

Beautiful night, charging along, no sail changes necessary! Wind around 20–25 knots SE, waves 2 meters with some bigger ones. Fun [to] watch them rolling under the boat. We spotted the oil platforms before sunrise, spouting occasional bursts of flame and then subsiding —pretty weird in the middle of the ocean. No sign of life except for the Australian planes buzzing us. Guess we will bypass Ashmore Reef as we will arrive around midnight tonight. Had to jibe, so we are on the less comfortable tack for 4 days. Why do we do this to ourselves? Sailing is crazy.

Another calm night, good sleeping! Running under full sails, dead downwind. Didn't have to do a thing all night. Still making good time, rolling less. Thomas caught a tuna this morning. We passed Ashmore Reef before midnight. Weather is too nice to stop. This is Tradewind sailing!

Lots of phosphorescence in the water last night, sparkly wake. Perfect 15–18 knot wind. Seas are way down. The others still have not left Darwin! Tranquility pulled into Ashmore this morning. Cloudless sky today! Charlotte is really trucking — averaging 7 knots for hours at a time. This is a sailing record for us!

Finally spotted some ships yesterday — 2 Indonesian boats going to windward, a big cargo at sunset, and one long-liner early in the morning. Another calm night, wind was down some but we still maintained 6 knots. Today we have up the mizzen and the yankee, making time while we can, anticipating lighter winds tonight as we approach the islands. 5 flying fish on deck this morning — I could hear them flopping at night. Need a cat!

Horrible current we have been bucking since the middle of last night, had to motor some to overcome it. Bali is cloud-covered, can't see the volcano. Approach is painful with big standing waves. We will be anchored by 10 am. All in all, a great sail!

Almost 2 weeks in Bali, it flew by. We tried to do as much as possible in the time we were there. Spent a week in the marina as the anchorage was poor and no other boats were there. Took a trip to the volcano and went on an elephant safari. Brian was so thrilled! Stumbled on to a kite-flying competition one day. The kites were huge — 30 feet wide, some with 200-foot tails, at least 10 men handled them, big line on a reel. The kites were launched to the accompaniment of brass gongs, wooden drum and gamelans (kind of like xylophones). It was a colorful scene. Most of the Balinese were dressed in 2 different sarongs, lots of black & white checks to represent the yin-yang of life. Tranquility arrived last Wednesday, Moonlight & Anke 2 on Tuesday. We took another drive with Rick & Mary to Ubud, then to a 1000-year-old temple at Gunung Kawi. We descended stone steps through rice paddies into a valley with a swift river flowing, with waterfalls along the rock face. The temple was carved out of the rock walls. It was magical. We loved the Balinese countryside, but the cities were loud and crowded with motor bikes. They call them 'mosquitoes' and they sure were pesky! So crowded everywhere and the street hawkers were obnoxious at times. We did get a lot of cool stuff though — silver earrings, wood carvings and paintings. The silk batik was absolutely fabulous, but I just enjoyed looking at it. We had fun buying DVDs for a dollar a piece! We would have stayed longer if the harbor had been nicer — the water was foul and the air stank like burning garbage. It was one of the nastiest ports we have ever been in — quite a disappointment. So now we are headed for Cocos Keeling, Bali is fading behind us and Java is just visible to starboard. The nets are full of delicious fruits for the week ahead. We are happy to have experienced Bali but glad to be in clear water again. The glimpses we got of Balinese culture were quite fascinating — temples everywhere. Big ornate ones, small ones in villages, tiny ones in individual yards. We were woken every morning at 5 am by the sound of Muslim singing. The occasional view of the volcano from the anchorage was nice. It was cool up there, with a big inviting lake. Won't forget the sight of peasants crouching in the rice fields with wooden salad bowls on their heads, women carrying concrete bricks on their heads, men in motorcycle helmets fishing in outrigger canoes. The people were small, good-looking, and friendly. They wondered how we could have skin color the same as theirs. Bali was an interesting place.

Calm night, beam reaching in 10 knots south wind, dodging long liners along the south coast of Java. Wind continues light today, still from the south. Pretty pleasant sailing conditions. Thomas caught the first mahi of the Indian Ocean early this morning. Brian started 8th grade today — it is painful to be a teacher again.

The stars were incredible last night — we will really miss the night skies of the Southern Hemisphere. Today has been a bit of a pain. Light, fluky winds, hard to steer the boat straight. A big cloud system looms and we can't get out from under it. So we sail some, then we bang around some. Keeps us busy though. Saw dolphins jumping — they were huge — 10 feet long. They came over to inspect the boat but found us too boring.

Another uneventful day at sea, just the way we like them! Wind was up this morning, did 8 knots for several hours before sunrise. Put a reef in the main for a few hours. The southerly swell got up to 3 meters while the wind was up.
Passed Christmas Island today — it was visible the entire day. Seagulls flying around. Wind 10–12 knots, speed down.

Wind died last night, after we passed Christmas Island and no longer had the option of stopping there. Less than 10 knots all night. It did not improve Thomas's disposition to hear that Bedouin and Just Jinx made it to Cocos in 3 days from Christmas. We are stuck in the wind hole for a day or so. No big deal really — it is pleasant enough out here, but we had hoped to be in Friday morning.

Another pleasant day at sea. Wind picked up enough last night so we were ghosting along at 5 knots, calm seas, very comfortable! Wind picked up enough today so we are doing 6 knots. Looks like we may be able to make it Friday after all.

Wind came up just before dinner last night — spoiled my enjoyment of the wine I had just opened! It was a bumpy, sleepless night, but we made good progress. The other boats made landfall in Cocos Keeling today, we will be in before noon tomorrow. Wind 20 knots today, squally, seas not quite as bad as last night.

We had planned to leave Cocos today, but a cyclone is sitting to the west of us and we had thunderstorms last night, so we are staying put. Arrived Fri Aug 13 at daybreak, what a beautiful place! We have enjoyed our 3 weeks here. Got to know some new people, Bob & Sue on Carefree, Christian & Fernanda on Bacanas from Brazil, Steve & Julie on Dos Tintos, Justin and Caroline with baby Sasha on Bonnie, Brian on Why Knot, Woody on Low Key. Had a great birthday party for Thomas, lots of people got drunk. Tranquility arrived and Brian is happy to spend time with Rick. Leo on Moonlight just arrived today. The days pass pleasantly. The water colors are all shades of turquoise, lots of palm trees ashore, a white sandy beach, a fun snorkel, cisterns with rain water, and a party area on shore. The boys windsurf. The South African boats Bedouin, Just Jinx and Golden Sovereign with Clive, Anne-Marie, Clare & Shaun were here when we arrived. Lots of socializing, happy hours every evening and several pot lucks. Bob on Carefree died yesterday at sea. Sue is still a day from Rodrigues, all alone with his body. I feel so sorry for her. We hope she makes it in safely tomorrow.

We finally tore ourselves away from Cocos yesterday. Had one more party Wed night. Forgot to mention Thomas' birthday bash where a lot of people got really drunk. Hans on Born Free could really hold his liquor! For my birthday, Rick set up his generator and TV on shore and we watched Captain Ron. Fidelio with Ian & Ann arrived, it was great to see them one last time, also Shadowfax with Tom & Serena. Several boats were planning to leave but only we & Bacanas made it out the pass, they going north to Chagos. It is quite rough, hard to do anything on board. 25 knots SE, big seas, but going fast..

Today is a bit easier — Thomas & I are feeling better. Still rough, but the wind is down a bit. If it wasn't for those southerly rollers, it wouldn't be so bad. The eggs went flying earlier — they have never fallen before. Forgot to mention 'the Rip' at Cocos — a cut with clear fast water and lots of fish — big fun to dive. I miss my exercise after 3 days of lying around, it is very wet on deck. You can up only be up there for short periods now. But the weather has cleared, we seem to have sailed out of the squalls, beautiful blue sky. The swells are still 10 feet, but the breaking seas are gone.

Always some excitement! The wind did back down last night after midnight as Mary on Tranquility had predicted. Thomas took the 2nd reef out. Soon after, we heard that awful sound — the sound of something breaking. The boom had broken in half at the vang fitting, which we had just replaced in Bali. We took the sail down, tied the boom to the deck, and went back to bed. A few hours later, at sunrise, Thomas whittled a piece of wood we picked up in Vanuatu to fit inside the boom. It was a perfect fit and we are back in business. The wind is down to 15–20 and seas are down to 2 meters. Sailing is much more comfortable and we can be outside without getting a shower.

We knew this would not be an easy trip, but we did not expect so much trouble. After a beautiful night with fog, a clear sky, and phosphorescent seas, we heard another horrible sound of breaking. This time it was the furler stay, something snapped at the top. We hanked a yankee on to the spare forestay, and we hope that the furler halyard will hold the weight for the next 10 days. It is impossible to go up the mast to inspect it in the rolling seas. Needless to say, morale is a bit low on board, we are all wondering what will happen next. Wind was around 20 knots when the furler busted and we were all out on deck.

Nothing broke in the last 24 hours, but we still passed a sleepless night, with the boat rolling, worrying, jumping up at every sound. Tied another halyard around the top of the furler this morning, to distribute the weight. Thomas made a splint for the boom from an old lifeline stanchion. Now we are sailing with yankee, staysail, full main & mizzen in 10–15 knots of wind, not too bad! Life goes on as usual.

Wind backed more to the east, so Thomas had to climb up the mast and put up a block for the spinnaker pole topping lift. For the first time we are using all the spare halyards on the main mast! Running under poled-out yankee was comfortable, we got to catch up on our sleep. Wind even more easterly today, so we are almost dead downwind, rolling a lot.

Hit the halfway mark yesterday around 8 pm. We celebrated with chocolate! Wind went light and easterly so our speed dropped, the boat rolled all night. For three days now I see the same bird at sunrise & sunset, flying behind the boat. Wonder where he goes during the day. Overcast all morning but now it is clearing up.

Another uneventful day, the way we like them! Lots of sunshine, wind easterly about 15 knots. Can tell the change in time zones, we were ready to go to sleep before the sun went down! Saw the new moon finally last night. The Indian Ocean sure is empty.

Another day, a lot of empty ocean. Getting tired of eating noodles and canned food! Brian is even beginning to burn out on reading. We have enough solar power to let him play computer games some. Can see the end now — 4 more days should get us to Rodrigues. Lots of empty ocean out here. Wind continues at 15–20, ESE to SE — pole out, pole down, reef occasionally. Trying to take it easy on the rig.

The wind started picking up last night at sundown, and howled and squalled all night. Then the big GPS died and it took us an hour to get the handheld going, as it had lost its memory and was reporting distance in statute miles. Sigh — what next? Wind is down today but we are still doing without the mainsail. Seas got big again. Sunny skies.

After an obnoxious night of sail changes and squalls with lots of rain, we finally settled on a sail plan of no main, double-reefed mizzen, 2 jibs. Blowing 20–25 with big rolling seas, but easterly so we are quite far off the wind. Wish it would calm down a bit for the last 2 days.

Rolling down the road, on the home stretch! Wind is down to 15 knots although seas are still big. Air is much warmer with the easterly winds. Last night was squally again but not as fierce. Other boats are having plenty of problems on this trip. Dos Tintos broke their Monitor self-steering, Sterling broke their self-steering and ripped the mainsail, Jean-Claude on La Brigne, who lost his Atom steering just 1 day out of Cocos, apparently hurt his head this morning but seems to be okay. There will be lots of wound-licking going on in Rodrigues! We still expect landfall early tomorrow morning if the wind does not die completely.

Land ho! Winds lightened during the night but we still rolled along. Turned ENE, had to jibe. Rolling was unbearable. But we are almost there. It was the fastest trip Charlotte has ever made — averaged over 150 miles a day. Will be happy to drop the hook. Hans on Born Free is still there, so we will have a familiar face.

Fun time in Rodrigues — it was an unexpectedly pleasant stop. When we arrived there was only Hans on Born Free and Pierre on Quo Vadis. By the time we left there were over a dozen boats. Many boats from Cocos — Dos Tintos with Steve & Julie, Shadowfax with Tom & Serena, Woody on Low Key, Jean-Claude on La Brigne, and a bunch of Dutch boats, including Sterling with Nick & Augette. The vegetables were so delicious — crisp and unfertilized, and Phoenix beer is tasty. We pigged out on baguettes, croissants, eclairs, custard horns. Big parties almost every night. I found a jeweler a Swiss guy — and had my Tuamotu carved pearls set. He invited us to his home for dinner. We took a day trip around the island with a bunch of other boaters — not much to see but we all had a good time. It was hard to leave but we were drinking too much. The town was very friendly, happy to have visitors. We fixed the forestay — Thomas made a new tang, and I patched the genoa. He spliced the boom with pieces of aluminium so it can't flex at all. We ordered a new GPS from Durban. Everyone was fixing stuff on their boats. Light winds forecast so we are off to Mauritius.

Very peaceful night, the way we like them. Winds 15 knots or less, poled out part of the time. Not going real fast, but don't care too, it's only a 350-mile trip. Only other ships out here are Tintos and the two Mauritius–Rodrigues supply boats.. Note: Helmut, Mila, & baby Amalie from Dillo jeweler — look up on internet

The Indian Ocean is blue and empty! Although Thomas did catch a mahi yesterday morning. Brian refuses to eat any more fish — too much on the Barrier Reef. Another quiet night, could see Dos Tintos all the time. 8 cargos passing N–S, right between us. Sang happy birthday to Julie on the VHF. The highlight of the day is Mary's Downwind Net, and email in the evening. Running as slow as comfortably possible so we don't arrive much before sunrise.

Made landfall at Port Louis, Mauritius, last Friday morning, along with Dos Tintos. Had to tie up along the wall at the marina, there was no other choice. Port Louis is a typical nasty 3rd world city, with some remnants of past colonial splendor. We took a bus trip with Tom & Serena off Shadowfax to center of the island. Looked at an unimpressive crater and a model boat factory with scale models of famous historical boats. Got stuck longer than we wanted in the marina when the wind died for 2 days. Finally left yesterday morning for Reunion. Trip started horribly with several hours of motoring into light head winds, then 25 knots hard to windward, before the wind finally backed and eased around sunset. Now we are rounding the south coast with a spectacular view of the mountain rising from the ocean up into the clouds.

Spent a pleasant week in St. Pierre at the marina. It blew a gale for several days, then died completely for a few days. I enjoyed swimming at the beach just past the breakwater. We took an exciting bus ride to a crater in the interior with Dos Tintos and hiked for a few hours. The roads were extremely narrow with tight hairpin curves, lots of near accidents! Reunion is quite lush and green. We enjoyed the best baguettes in the world. Had several dinners and happy hours, time passed quickly. Left today at noon with a light southerly wind, can't quite hold the course. Tintos & Stella Maris left with us.

A couple of small squalls last night — the wind died completely then came back with all sails backed. Did okay until sunrise when it lightened again. Now motoring for a few hours since we can't hold the course to windward. Guess this is going to be a long slow sail! At least we have lots of good food this time, plenty of beer. Other boats are out of sight. Water very blue. Enjoying the hot sun while I still can!

Peaceful night, beautiful morning. Thomas had to call a freighter last night so they changed course to avoid us. Wind backed to the east so we are poled out with 4 sails up, still making 3 knots or less. Hope the wind will come up some tonight. It is comfortable at least! [24]-hour run — 107 miles

We cruised most of the night with the mizzen drifter up, 2 headsails, and full main. Took it down when the wind picked up early morning. We have seen 5 knots occasionally today. Dos Tintos is slowly pulling ahead, Stella Maris falling behind. Woody got to Durban, 18 days from Rodrigues, with wind over 20 K.

Had to jibe yesterday evening — what a hassle. The roll on the starboard tack kept us awake most of the night. The wind has backed to the north now and we are broad reaching at 5.5 knots. More comfortable now. At least the north wind is warm!

Woke up to north winds, then they backed to NW. Had to motor for a few hours until the wind came around to the south. We are happy to be back on 'Charlotte tack'! Talked to Pierre on Quo Vadis this morning, he is only 40 miles ahead of us. We are hard on the wind but hoping it will turn to SE soon.

Great sailing for a change! Picked up current before sunset and did 7 knots for a few hours. Wind backed more to the east so we put up the pole at sunrise, making good time with 4 sails. Gaining on Dos Tintos now. Stella Maris & Sterling are behind us. Weather forecast looks good for the next 5 days. It has been a warm sunny day after an overcast, drizzly night.

Today is not a wonderful day — the sun is shining, 15K wind from the wrong direction. We tried motorsailing for a while, but were making little progress against the wind and current. We did see a whale this afternoon and we have had booby birds with us all day. Morale is not very high here, but we trying to keep it together.

Happy Halloween! The gale hit today. Motored all night, made good progress for a change. Lucky for us, Dos Tintos warned us of the approaching SW gale. Been in it now for several hours, seas are building now, we have up staysail, no. 2 yankee, double-reefed mizzen, doing 6½ knots. It's a bit too much for me. But we are making progress.

It was quite a night. Second front line hit around 8 pm and blew 40 knots for a while. We had to dump the staysail in a hurry. It was wild out, took hours for Thomas to get the nerve to go back out there when the wind abated. The weather has turned much cooler. Today at sunrise the wind backed to east of south so we are sailing upright again. Everyone had a wild ride last night! We talk every morning on Pierre's net as well as Mary's.

Last night was perfect, until around 3 am when the wind started dying. We were poled out with 4 sails, got to catch up on our sleep! Today has been very light, motored for a few hours, now waiting for the wind to come back up. It is slow, about 3½, but even Thomas is sick of the sound of the engine. It is fun having all the morning net schedules — everyone else is waiting for wind too.

Thought we had clear sailing from here on in to the coast — ha! A coastal low has developed, coming up, blowing 20–25 SW so far. Sterling of course is nervous about it blowing a gale, and there were some gale reports, we don't know where. We are talking every few hours with the South African nets and with our friends. Quo Vadis & Tintos are hove to, Sterling is sailing east. We keep on going, we are west of all of them. Chances are it won't amount to much, but no one feels like taking chances. Now that we finally have a good wind and a favorable current, it is difficult to slow down. Tintos was surrounded by 6 whales today, it was cool but also rather frightening for them. We would have been thrilled! So we will see what the night will bring, not much sleep, that's for sure.
entries.conditions: 24-hour run — 139 miles — Perfect night last night, 15 SE — full sails

entries.body: Front never came through last night, clouds came in around 3 am and wind died. Today we have light west winds, so we are motoring the last 50 miles, get to sail some at 8 knots with the current, wind is variable. Finally made out the African coastline about 22 miles off. We will be in sometime this afternoon. It has been an aggravating trip!
